name: Narodniks
summary: Narodism (narodnichestvo) was the Russian agrarian-socialist current of the 1860s to 1880s whose intelligentsia idealised the peasantry and held that the village commune could carry Russia to socialism without passing through capitalism. Its thinkers, from Herzen and Chernyshevsky to Lavrov and Mikhailovsky, wanted the autocracy overthrown, land in the hands of the cultivators and self-governing communes, and differed over methods from peaceful propaganda to terror. It had no single doctrine, so the sources settle only some test questions.

scope: The classical Russian Narodnik current as the defining sources describe it: Herzen and Chernyshevsky as its intellectual founders, the theorists Lavrov and Mikhailovsky, and the going-to-the-people movement of the 1870s, with its faith in the narod and the peasant commune and its claim that Russia could bypass capitalism (Klid, Encyclopedia of Ukraine; Young; New World Encyclopedia). It excludes the Narodnaya Volya party's programme as a separate organisation, Tkachev's Jacobin strand which Young places at the edge of Populism, Ukrainian populism's national programme, and the Socialist Revolutionary party.

missingStatements.text: A country can reach socialism without first passing through a capitalist stage.
missingStatements.rationale: The defining sources present bypassing capitalism through the peasant commune as the central tenet of Narodism.

quotes.text: By modernizing and building on the commune, Russia could bypass capitalist development and move directly to the next, higher stage, socialism.
quotes.where: Klid, paragraph on Russian populism as ideology

quotes.text: the Narodniks generally believed that capitalism was not a necessary result of industrial development, and that it was possible to skip capitalism altogether, and enter straight into a kind of socialism.

notes: Themes searched: land and the commune (Herzen, Klid, Young, Stepniak), capitalism, state and federation, violence and revolution, religion, welfare, the political-rights and constitution questions (only Narodnaya Volya's programme speaks to these and it is a separate organisation, so they stay null), economy and trade (Lenin's critique quotes Narodniks but a critic's quotations are not checked against the originals), and the nation and minorities (Klid says most Russian populists did not consider the national question important). Lavrov's Historical Letters and Mikhailovsky's What Is Progress? could not be fetched as full text, so their positions rest on Young's report of Walicki and Copleston. The movement had no single doctrine (Klid), so many statements stay null.
